body: my advice to everyone: don't try to prove it right, that's the wrong approach.

The rules are very simple: for each token, generate a probability distribution without looking at the answer. If you vibe code an algorithm so complex that you can't tell if its looking at the answer before predicting, there is a simple automated way to test:

1. mask out a random position in the validation set. 
2. Run your TTT and scoring method, log your prediction for the masked token.
3. Repeat with the unmasked dataset, and confirm the prediction matches exactly.
4. Repeat N times with different masked tokens.

Given how many submissions are illegal, it may help if someone writes this automated testing framework, and it then gets adopted as a requirement for submissions.

I think this compresses several distinct obligations into one slogan and then proposes a test for only one of them.

There is a charitable reading under which your sentence really does contain the whole thing. If by "generate a probability distribution without looking at the answer" you mean: define a full normalized distribution over the official token alphabet using only the submitted artifact and the strict prefix; fix that position's score contribution before any `x_t`-dependent update or accounting rule is allowed; and report one committed evaluation rather than best-of-`k` after seeing outcomes, then yes, that is my four conditions in one line.

But that is not what the masking harness, as written, actually checks.

What it checks is one useful special case: whether changing `x_t` changes the prediction at position `t`. That is a worthwhile sanity check for same-position leakage. It is not a complete test for legality.

In particular, it does not test full causal dependence. A predictor can ignore `x_t` completely and still peek at `x_{t+1}` or any later token. Masking only the current position will not catch that. This does not, by the way, show Condition 1 is insufficient; it shows the proposed harness is insufficient as a test for Condition 1.

More importantly, it misses Condition 2. "Not looking at the answer" is about information flow. Condition 2 is about the type of object being scored. A submission can be perfectly causal and still fail to define a single full normalized distribution over the official alphabet. It can normalize over buckets rather than tokens, score only a shortlist, define only the realized-token score, or otherwise fail to commit the counterfactual probabilities that make log-loss a code length. 

And as stated, the harness leaves under-specified what exactly is being compared: a single reported score, a top prediction, or the full distribution. That ambiguity is not incidental. It is exactly the gap Condition 2 is there to close. If you repair the harness by requiring the full vector over the official alphabet and checking normalization, you have added Condition 2 back in by hand.

Condition 3 also does independent work once one distinguishes the distribution from the accounting. A submission can compute a perfectly legal causal distribution, and then use `x_t` to decide whether that position is counted, downweighted, clipped, or otherwise treated specially in the reported `val_bpb`. The distribution was legal, but the bookkeeping was not. Condition 1 constrains the distribution. Condition 2 constrains what kind of object it is. Neither, on its own, forbids `x_t`-dependent scoring rules unless you say so explicitly.

Condition 4 is different again. Its independent role is not two-pass cache laundering; if future tokens enter a run's state, that is clearly already a Condition 1 problem. The clean independence argument is outcome selection. You can run thirty fully legal evaluations, each individually satisfying Conditions 1–3, and then report the best one. No single run looked ahead. The illegality is at the outer protocol level: the final score was chosen using observed validation outcomes. PR #844 did exactly this.

So I am not against the harness. I think it would be useful, and I would support adding it as a diagnostic. But it is not a replacement for the conditions. If you expand it enough to perturb arbitrary suffix tokens, log the full distribution over the official alphabet, verify normalization, check that the position's contribution is fixed independently of `x_t`-dependent accounting, and rule out best-of-`k` outcome selection, then it becomes a decent implementation aid. Altough at that point it is no longer an alternative to the four conditions. It is a partial enforcement mechanism for them.

I hope this wasn't too heavy-handed. You raised good points and the harness idea has real merit. My concern is that the agents are reading these threads with the same enthusiasm they bring to reading top PRs, and if they latch onto "just mask and compare" as the complete validity check, we'll be drowning in a new flavor of confidently wrong submissions by Tuesday. So thank you for the pushback! And sorry for replying at a length that probably violates some kind of compression constraint.

This is the compliance document the competition needed from day one.

The four conditions are rigorous and actionable — especially Condition 2 (full normalized distribution), which is the one that killed the most submissions in the March 27 sweep. You've been the one actually enforcing this across PRs (#995, #986, others) and now you've formalized it.

The Track A / Track B distinction is valuable. Right now everything gets lumped together — a fixed predictor and an adaptive compressor are fundamentally different achievements but compete on the same leaderboard. Making that explicit would help both participants and reviewers.

We've incorporated your framework into [AGORA](https://matotezitanka.github.io/parameter-golf/) (our community companion site). The checklist section already covers the basics, but we're planning to upgrade it to reference your 4 conditions explicitly and split the leaderboard by Track A / Track B in a future update.

One thing that would strengthen this: concrete code snippets showing what a Condition 2 violation looks like vs a correct implementation. The entropy expert example in the table is good but a before/after code diff would make it agent-proof. You mentioned wanting agents to read this and self-correct — giving them a pattern to match against is the most effective way.

Strong +1 for turning this into a `CONTRIBUTING.md` PR.

*Disclosure: I use Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI, and Gemini Pro as tools in my workflow. Human first, AI-assisted.*

> You raised good points and the harness idea has real merit. My concern is that the agents are reading these threads with the same enthusiasm they bring to reading top PRs, and if they latch onto "just mask and compare" as the complete validity check, we'll be drowning in a new flavor of confidently wrong submissions by Tuesday.

Realistically, the verbosity of your conditions will be useful for agents and people who are submitting PRs without understanding what their code is doing or have never done ML. The 'charitable reading' you mentioned would be how anyone in the space would read it, as a probability distribution by definition must sum to 1, and intermediate tensors that get manipulated with ensembles or second pass updates are not the single 'generated probability distribution'.

However, I recognize that this competition has brought in a huge flood of people to the space, which is overall a very good thing. And this new audience benefits from a different level of elaboration of the rules.

As you mention, the recommended harness isn't an enforcement of the rules, just a sanity test for the honest participant who is trying to debug the code their agent wrote. Someone can make a more comprehensive harness.

Not proposing a new validity rule here, just a separation of layers.

A useful separation here is between:

1. the validity conditions for `val_bpb`,
2. the enforcement harnesses used to detect violations,
3. the evidence surface that reviewers and tools inspect.

A masking harness can be useful for one class of failures without being a complete validity test. That seems compatible with the four-condition framing.

Separately, an optional, review-side, machine-readable evidence surface for (3) could make review less brittle without changing what counts toward the submission artifact: artifact accounting, evaluation metadata, training/evaluation wall-clock measurements, statistical evidence, and provenance in one place.

That would not replace the conditions, and it would not replace targeted harnesses. Its role would be narrower: reduce reconstruction from PR text, `README.md`, `submission.json`, and logs.
